title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts
keywords: Appendix C: A Prelude to Paperless Courts
primary_topics: Appendix C of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's opening remarks 'A Prelude to Paperless Courts,' delivered September 26, 2001 introducing a Centenary Lecture by Justice Robert Nicholson of the Federal Court of Australia on 'Paperless Courts: The Australian Experience'

A survey of the new-millennium paradigms transforming even 'the normally reclusive and exclusive judicial enclaves' -- the shift from ideologies and weapons to trade dominance, from government control to deregulation, privatization, globalization and trade liberalization, and the rise of the Information Age and the biosciences

The provocative proposition of eliminating paper from 'the most paper-dependent discipline in the world,' where rules like parol evidence, the statute of frauds and best evidence all assume documentation written on paper

The concrete legal milestone: with RA 8792 (the Electronic Commerce Act, 2000) and the Philippine Rules on Electronic Evidence (effective August 1, 2001), an electronic document becomes the functional equivalent of a paper one and a digital signature the equivalent of a penned signature -- making the Supreme Court 'one of the first tribunals in Asia' to keep step with the electronic age
sub_topics: The occasion: opening remarks before the centenary lecture 'Paperless Courts: The Australian Experience' by Justice Robert Nicholson of the Federal Court of Australia, in the SC Session Hall on September 26, 2001

The macro-shifts of the new millennium: the contest for world preeminence moving from ideologies and weapons to trade dominance, and strategy shifting 'from government control to deregulation, from state ownership to privatization, from national sovereignty to globalization, and from protectionism to trade liberalization'

The Information Age: computer technologies hastening the industrial era's obsolescence, with information transmitted via the Internet and fiber optics becoming 'as valuable as oil resources, gold mines, heavy industries and agricultural products'
The biosciences: cloning, extra-womb stem-cell development, DNA testing and genetic engineering promising longer lives (150 or even 200 years) while raising ethical and moral concerns

The challenge to the judiciary: these developments transform 'everything else that matters,' including the judicial enclaves -- and the specific 'transformational shift' under discussion is the elimination of paper

Law as the most paper-dependent discipline: 'Put it in writing' assumes paper, and rules on parol evidence, the statute of frauds and best evidence 'show a definite bias in favor of documentation' on paper (the Ten Commandments in stone, Confucian wisdom in wooden tablets, but written communication long assumed to mean paper)

The legal milestone: RA 8792, the Electronic Commerce Act (passed June 11, 2000), and the Philippine Rules on Electronic Evidence (effective August 1, 2001) eliminate the 'disparity of treatment between data messages and paper documents,' making an electronic document the functional equivalent of a paper one and an electronic/digital signature the equivalent of a penned 'John Hancock'

The measured conclusion: the Court is proud to be 'one of the first tribunals in Asia' to adopt such rules, but there is 'as yet no intention... to eliminate paper as the primary medium' -- the lecture would assess whether paperless courts are truly possible in the Philippines

stances.claim: The judiciary cannot remain insulated from the new-millennium paradigms -- globalization, the Information Age and the biosciences -- that are transforming 'everything else that matters'; even 'the most paper-dependent discipline in the world' must reckon with the elimination of paper, and the Court's adoption of the Electronic Commerce Act framework and the Rules on Electronic Evidence shows it keeping 'in step with the electronic age.'
stances.rhetorical_move: paradigm-shift framing: situating a technical evidentiary reform within a sweeping account of global and scientific change to argue the courts must modernize
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's forward-looking institutional stance

stances.claim: Modernization is incremental, not revolutionary: the new Rules make an electronic document the 'functional equivalent' of a paper one and a digital signature the equivalent of a penned signature, but there is 'as yet no intention... to eliminate paper as the primary medium of communication in the bar or the bench.' -- reform that admits new media without discarding the old.
stances.rhetorical_move: functional-equivalence with restraint: embracing electronic evidence while disclaiming any abrupt abolition of paper to reassure a paper-bound profession
stances.confidence: stated as the Court's measured position

notable_anecdotes: Stone, wood, and paper: CJP observes that 'the Ten Commandments may have been engraved in stone and Confucian wisdom in wooden tablets,' but until recently the law has always assumed that 'something shall be in writing' means written on paper -- a bias built into parol-evidence, statute-of-frauds and best-evidence rules.

Information as the new oil: he frames the Information Age by noting that data transmitted via the Internet and fiber optics has become 'as valuable as oil resources, gold mines, heavy industries and agricultural products.'

200-year lifespans: surveying the biosciences -- cloning, stem cells, DNA testing, genetic engineering -- CJP suggests 'our children and grandchildren can look forward to much longer life spans of 150 or even 200 years.'

First in Asia: he reports the Supreme Court's pride at being 'one of the first tribunals in Asia' to promulgate Rules on Electronic Evidence under the Electronic Commerce Act -- while candidly disclaiming any present intention to abolish paper.

one_paragraph_summary: Appendix C of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's opening remarks, 'A Prelude to Paperless Courts,' delivered September 26, 2001 to introduce a centenary lecture by Justice Robert Nicholson of the Federal Court of Australia on the Australian paperless-courts experience. CJP surveys the new-millennium paradigms reshaping the world -- the contest for preeminence shifting from ideologies and weapons to trade dominance, and strategy moving 'from government control to deregulation, from state ownership to privatization, from national sovereignty to globalization, and from protectionism to trade liberalization' -- alongside the Information Age (where data via the Internet and fiber optics is 'as valuable as oil resources') and the biosciences (cloning, stem cells, DNA, lifespans of 150-200 years). These forces, he argues, transform even 'the normally reclusive and exclusive judicial enclaves.' He then turns to the provocative idea of eliminating paper from 'the most paper-dependent discipline in the world,' where 'Put it in writing' assumes paper and rules like parol evidence, the statute of frauds and best evidence carry 'a definite bias in favor of documentation.' The concrete milestone is legal: with RA 8792 (the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000) and the Philippine Rules on Electronic Evidence (effective August 1, 2001), an electronic document becomes the 'functional equivalent' of a paper one and a digital signature the equivalent of a penned 'John Hancock' -- making the Supreme Court 'one of the first tribunals in Asia' to keep step with the electronic age. CJP closes with measured restraint, noting there is 'as yet no intention... to eliminate paper as the primary medium,' and welcoming the lecture as 'the epochal prelude to paperless legal proceedings in our country.'
